definition: Heterodox means contrary to accepted or established belief.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word heterodox. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know heterodox should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her heterodox training plan — rest days before races, no morning runs — contradicted nearly everything the coaching manuals prescribed.
Questioning merely asks whether the accepted view holds; it stops well short of heterodox.
Dissenting goes further than questioning — it openly disagrees — but usually with one decision; heterodox sets a whole position against the established doctrine itself.

Nonconforming means declining to follow the group's practices — dress, ritual, procedure — in behavior as much as in belief. Heterodox is narrower and aims at doctrine: a heterodox position sets its claims against the established teaching itself. You can be nonconforming in what you wear; you are heterodox only in what you believe.

Unorthodox says a method or choice departs from standard practice — an unorthodox batting stance, an unorthodox route to a degree. Heterodox is the heavier, doctrinal cousin: it stands against a settled body of accepted belief, so there must be an orthodoxy to defy. A technique can be unorthodox; a theology or a theory is heterodox.

Heterodox is more precise than 'unconventional' because it points at belief: it means contrary to accepted or established doctrine, so there has to be an orthodoxy — a settled teaching — for a position to stand against.
A strange haircut is unconventional; a theory the whole field rejects is heterodox.
Heterodox lives in academic and religious argument, where a settled doctrine exists to stand against; it describes positions and thinkers, not haircuts.

The scandal was never her conduct; it was her theory.
